articles.title: Two brain circuits coordinate fruit flies' wing and leg movements to threaten rivals
articles.description: Limbs evolved as a means of locomotion. From the primitive rotating flagella of bacteria to the wings of flies and even our own legs, animals use these appendages to travel to find food or mates or escape predators. But in countless species across the animal kingdom, limbs are repurposed to create elaborate social displays: Birds of paradise fan out their wings and hop around in courtship dances, while crabs wave their claws to communicate to potential mating partners. As humans, we use our limbs to dance, gesture while talking, wield tools and conduct a remarkable diversity of behaviors. How does the brain control and coordinate its body parts for such distinct purposes?

articles.title: Mini Organs Launching to Space For Study On Aging
articles.description: Researchers from Mount Sinai, NASA, and Space Tango have launched miniature human hearts and brains to the International Space Station to study how microgravity and radiation affect organs and potentially accelerate aging. "If people are going to be living and working in space, then we need to understand what's going to happen to them," David Sachs, assistant professor of surgery at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. "But also, because it's interesting as a model of accelerated aging for studying people on Earth." From the report: The mini organs launched aboard commercial resupply mission CRS-35 on Tuesday morning from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. They are expected to arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday. The miniature organs offer researchers a unique opportunity to simulate aging in a much shorter period of time to understand disease and develop treatments. "Six months in space ... is equivalent to about 10 to 20 years of aging on Earth," Kevin Costa, associate professor of surgery at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. Sachs and Costa are sending up to 16 miniature hearts to the ISS to test how they respond to electrical signals and monitor how they may react to near-zero gravity. The technology, which is integrated into a miniature laboratory called CubeLab, was developed by Space Tango and simulates the natural environment in the human body. "[It is] slightly bigger than a shoebox, and it is a fully automated, miniaturized system," Gentry Barnett, chief technology officer at Space Tango, told ABC News. [...] As part of the new effort, the team is sending miniature brains, called miBrain, to the ISS. Around the size of a peppercorn, the miBrains reflect models of healthy and diseased brains. By exposing them to the space environment, scientists can see how mini-brains respond and better understand why living in space accelerates aging. Though the mini organs are not full-sized human organs, the researchers say they are good substitutes, cost-effective and don't take up much of the limited space aboard the space station. They also believe discoveries made in space can translate to uses in everyday medical care. The microgravity environment uniquely allows researchers to study what happens to humans with a sedentary lifestyle or prolonged bed rest, which isn't easily simulated on Earth, Sachs explained. "[The research is] translating to stuff in space, but it's also translating back to the research we do in the laboratory to help people with Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease," Joel Blanchard, associate professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine and neuroscience at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. Lisa Carnell, the director of the biological and physical sciences division at NASA, told ABC News that these experiments serve as a starting point for future research beyond low Earth orbit, including to the moon and beyond. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Protesters call for justice at Patterson Park following Cornell rape allegations
articles.description: On Oct. 8, 2026 approximately 40 demonstrators gathered at Patterson Park Observatory in Baltimore to support survivors and demand greater institutional accountability following the recent allegations of sexual violence at Cornell University. The protest began at 5 p.m. Demonstrators held signs reading "We are Jane Doe" and "I am Jane Doe" as they followed one of the co-organizers, Ally Donovan, in chanting, "We love you. We believe you. We will fight for you." Throughout the rally, survivors of sexual violence and their supporters delivered speeches addressing the impact of sexual assault, calling for greater support and solidarity with survivors. Donovan is a graduate student at the Bloomberg School of Public Health. In an interview with The News-Letter, she said that the protest aimed to provide a space for Baltimore residents to express solidarity with survivors amid recent national attention to campus sexual violence. "Our intention was to bring the community in general together to support sexual violence survivors… and to ensure that we hold a space here in Baltimore where survivors can gather with the difficult times that we're experiencing right now with everything in the news cycle," she said. Donovan further explained that the demonstration was intended to show solidarity with Jane Doe, the former Cornell student whose lawsuit has drawn national attention, and Kendall Francis, a Louisiana State University student who has publicly challenged her university's handling of a sexual assault complaint. The protest was titled "From the Frat House to the White House: Stop Sexual Violence," and it was part of a national day of action organized by Women's March, me too. International, Feminist Generation and FEMINIST. The national demonstrations followed a civil lawsuit filed on Sept. 16 by a former Cornell student identified under the pseudonym Jane Doe. The lawsuit alleges that seven members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her in October 2024 after she consumed alcohol and was pressured into taking ketamine. Cornell's internal disciplinary proceedings resulted in the expulsion of two students and the suspension of two others. No criminal charges have been filed against the accused in connection with the allegations. After local prosecutors reopened the investigation on Sept. 28, New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to investigate this incident. So far, all of the seven men denied wrongdoing, and none have faced criminal charges. Moonies Bar & Nightclub denied serving Jane Doe alcohol when she was underage. Beyond the Cornell case, the national campaign called for stronger Title IX enforcement, expanded campus support services for survivors of sexual violence and the abolition of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. At Patterson Park, participants also emphasized the importance of community support and institutional responsibility. For Edith, a student at Baltimore School for the Arts, the protest offered an opportunity to connect with others who shared her concerns. "I've heard a lot about everything that's going on right now, and I just have a lot of feelings about it," she said to The News-Letter. "And I wanted to be surrounded by people who also have the same feelings." Teresa Lancaster, an attorney, advocate and survivor who attended the protest, emphasized the need for strong protections against sexual violence in institutions such as churches and universities in an interview with The News-Letter. "These universities need to take a stronger look into what goes on and stop brushing it over just because a lot of the students have money," Lancaster said. Despite her concerns about institutional accountability, Lancaster expressed optimism about the demonstration's potential impact. "I'm very delighted to see many people turn out and recognize that this was wrong, that [it] needs to be right," she said. "[I've] been fighting for it all my life, and we're seeing it."

articles.title: SGA discusses budget and potential transfer student caucus
articles.description: On Tuesday, Oct. 13 the Student Government Association (SGA) convened for its eighth general body meeting of the semester. The meeting began with the Senate's confirmation of two new justices to SGA's judiciary, junior Jonathan Aguilar and senior Jacqueline Kim. After the new justices were confirmed, the meeting's agenda was approved. During the designated time for public input, a representative from the CARE Club made an announcement about a Halloween event that CARE and SGA would be collaborating on. The meeting then moved into reports from the executive branch of SGA, as well as a report from the SGA Advisor about a planned social event for SGA senators. Then the meeting allowed for individual reports from senators, during which Senator Paul Woo gave a report on potentially replacing two-factor authentication with passkeys on University Wi-Fi, as well as the possibility of establishing a community garden on the Homewood campus. President of the Senate Jazzlyn Fernandez then announced that SGA members in attendance would be nominating a Senator of the Month for September. Student Athlete Caucus Chair Sophia Baleeiro was chosen for the title. Senator Peter Tarpley then gave a presentation about the state of SGA's budget, in which he shared that SGA is slightly overspending and advised a weekly spending budget of $4,500. The meeting then entered legislative procedures. Vice President of the Senate Shreeman Patel introduced a bill for first reading about the establishment of a caucus for transfer students, which was referred to the Internal Affairs Committee. Senator Paul Woo then introduced a bill aiming to amend the bylaws to explicitly appoint a member of SGA to the University's Cross-Institutional Student Advisory Committee (CSAC,) an advisory board made of students from all of the University's campuses. The bill was also referred to the Internal Affairs Committee after a moderated caucus, in which SGA members mentioned that Sophomore Class President Veda Kommineni already serves as SGA's appointee to the CSAC. Senator Sophia Baleeiro also introduced a bill to fund T-shirts for the Student Athlete Advisory Council, which was referred to the Finance Committee. Sophomore Class President Veda Kommineni then discussed her bill, which was in its second reading. The bill focused on a tabling event for SGA, in which students will be able to give feedback to SGA. The committee then motioned for a moderated caucus to discuss whether an online survey or index cards were the best method to gather feedback. After Kommineni's bill was passed, the meeting moved into cohort time and then adjourned.
